name: Neurocutaneous melanosis
aliases: leptomeningeal melanosis with congenital melanocytic naevi

reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Neurocutaneous Disorders (current reference texts)
clinicalPearls: Defined by large or multiple congenital melanocytic naevi together with abnormal melanocytic proliferation in the leptomeninges
Risk is highest with a large or giant congenital melanocytic naevus in a posterior axial (head, neck or spine) location and with numerous satellite naevi
Caused by post-zygotic activating variants, most often in NRAS, affecting neural-crest-derived melanocyte precursors
Many affected children are neurologically asymptomatic, but leptomeningeal melanosis can cause raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus
Presenting neurological features include seizures, developmental delay, cranial nerve palsies and signs of a mass lesion
There is a significant risk of central nervous system melanoma arising within the abnormal leptomeningeal melanocytes
Management is generic and supportive: neuroimaging surveillance, treatment of hydrocephalus and seizures, and oncological referral if melanoma develops
reference.pathophysiology: Neurocutaneous melanosis results from a post-zygotic activating variant, most commonly in NRAS, occurring in a neural-crest melanocyte precursor early in embryogenesis. The affected clone gives rise both to large or multiple congenital melanocytic naevi in the skin and to an excess of melanocytes that populate the leptomeninges. Proliferation of these leptomeningeal melanocytes can impair cerebrospinal fluid flow, producing hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure, and may undergo malignant transformation into central nervous system melanoma. The shared NRAS driver explains the concurrence of extensive cutaneous pigmentation and intracranial melanocytic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated large congenital melanocytic naevus without CNS involvement
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and spine, ideally in infancy before myelination obscures melanin signal, to detect leptomeningeal melanosis
Assessment for hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure
Cerebrospinal fluid cytology where malignant transformation is suspected
Skin examination to map the number and distribution of congenital melanocytic naevi
Molecular testing of naevus tissue for NRAS variants where available
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure or rapidly enlarging head circumference
New seizures, focal deficit or cranial nerve palsy
Any feature suggesting central nervous system melanoma
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely: asymptomatic children may remain well, but symptomatic leptomeningeal disease carries a guarded outlook, and the development of central nervous system melanoma is associated with a poor prognosis despite treatment.
pitfalls: Focusing only on cutaneous naevi and not arranging early MRI in high-risk patients
Delaying imaging until after infancy when myelination reduces sensitivity for melanin
Attributing hydrocephalus to other causes and missing leptomeningeal melanosis
Underestimating the melanoma risk in symptomatic disease
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
management: Establish the extent of disease with neuraxis MRI in infancy and characterise the cutaneous naevi to guide prognosis and monitoring
Relieve symptomatic hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure with cerebrospinal fluid diversion such as a ventriculoperitoneal shunt
Undertake surveillance for malignant transformation with clinical review and neuroimaging, and cerebrospinal fluid cytology where central nervous system melanoma is suspected
Manage established central nervous system melanoma palliatively through a neuro-oncology team, as it responds poorly to treatment
Address the cutaneous naevi with dermatological monitoring and consider surgical management for melanoma risk and cosmesis
Provide multidisciplinary neurology, dermatology and neurosurgical care with developmental support and family counselling
